cards.title: Fridge & Freezer / Cold Chain Checks
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- say what the cold chain is
- check and record fridge and freezer temperatures
- use and store food so it stays cold

cards.title: The cold chain
cards.body: The cold chain is the unbroken run of cold temperatures that keeps food safe from delivery to the moment it is cooked or served. Every link matters. If food warms up at any point, bacteria get the chance to multiply, and you cannot always see or smell the difference.

cards.title: Check and record
cards.body: At the start of each day, and often through it, check and record fridge and freezer temperatures. Writing the readings down is not box-ticking. It is how we catch a failing unit early, before a whole fridge of stock has to be thrown away or, worse, served.

cards.title: Let the cold air move
cards.body: How you use the units matters. Do not overload them or block the vents, because that stops cold air circulating and creates warm spots. Keep doors closed as much as possible.

left.title: Do
items: Leave room for air to move

cards.title: Put it away quickly
cards.body: When a delivery arrives, put chilled and frozen items away quickly rather than leaving them out on the pass to warm up.

cards.title: Raw below, oldest first
cards.body: Keep raw meat stored below ready-to-eat foods so nothing drips down, and rotate stock so older items get used first.

cards.title: Report it immediately
cards.body: If a unit is running warm, do not ignore it. Report it immediately and check the food inside. Acting fast can be the difference between a quick repair and a food-poisoning risk.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Fridges 5°C or below, freezers -18°C or below
- Check and record at least daily, and write it down
- Do not overload or block vents; keep doors shut
- Put deliveries away quickly; raw meat stored below ready-to-eat
- A warm unit is reported immediately, and the food is checked

cards.why: Fridges should run at 5°C or below.

cards.q: Freezers should be at -18°C or below.
cards.why: -18°C or below is the freezer target.

options: A list of our approved suppliers
A chain of command for cold stock
Unbroken cold from delivery to use
The order that dishes are cooked in
cards.why: Every link matters from delivery to the moment food is cooked or served.

cards.q: Overloading a fridge can block airflow and create warm spots.
cards.why: Blocked vents and overloading stop cold air circulating.

cards.q: How often should fridge/freezer temperatures be checked and recorded?
options: Only when a unit looks warm
cards.why: Check and record at the start of each day, and often through it.

cards.q: When a delivery arrives, chilled items should be put away quickly.
cards.why: Leaving them out on the pass lets them warm up.
Stored below, nothing can drip down onto ready-to-eat food.

cards.q: If a unit is running warm you should ignore it if it's busy.
cards.why: Report it immediately and check the food. Acting fast can prevent a food-poisoning risk.

cards.q: Why do we write down (record) the temperatures rather than just checking?
options: To catch a failing unit early and prove food is safe
To fill in time between services
To avoid checking the next day
cards.why: Records catch a failing unit before stock is thrown away or served, and show food is kept safe.

cards.q: Leaving fridge doors open for long periods helps keep energy costs down.
cards.why: Keep doors closed as much as possible so the cold stays in.
